title: Do Verifiers Reduce Security-Relevant Misconfigurations? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Verifier-in-the-Loop GVR for Intent-to-Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired experiment (N = 300 matched intents; 150 benign + 150 programmatic adversarial variants) to test whether embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline. Under the executed adapter contract each pair used a single shared initial LLM candidate (model_calls_used = 300) replayed to both arms. Two deterministic validators (a containerized Batfish-style execution validator and a lightweight graph-based static reachability analyzer) were combined with a logical-OR decision rule; repair was allowed up to one LLM call per pair if any validator detected forbidden reachability. The run completed all planned episodes (planned = 600, completed = 600, failed = 0). Observed outcomes were degenerate: baseline_success_count = 300 and guarded_success_count = 300 (contingency n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0), McNemar exact two-sided p = 1.0, bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) 95% CI for paired risk-difference = [0.0, 0.0]. Because no validator reported forbidden reachability, the repair path was never invoked and the confirmatory hypothesis about repair efficacy is untestable in this run; the one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on an undetected baseline violation rate is ≈0.00994. The manuscript compresses provenance pointers (full archived artifacts available in the evidence bundle) and focuses on (1) the degenerate empirical outcome and its statistical interpretation, (2) explicit, artifact-grounded design lessons (generation semantics, adversary potency, verifier strength, and repair budget), and (3) reproducibility materials and recommendations for follow-up stress tests intended to exercise the repair path.

sections.introduction: LLMs are increasingly proposed to automate intent-driven network configuration, but operational deployment raises concrete safety concerns: generated artifacts can expand attack surface, violate access-control policies, or produce other security-regressing changes. Prior system and survey work therefore recommends constrained generation, execution-oracle validation, and iterative generate–verify–repair (GVR) loops as mitigations. We asked a focused operational question and preregistered a confirmatory design: Does embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a GVR loop reduce the incidence of forbidden-reachability misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline? Our contributions are (1) a preregistered paired confirmatory experiment (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) executed deterministically in Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation with two deterministic validators and shared_initial_candidate generation semantics; (2) a compact reporting of the degenerate empirical outcome (n11 = 300) together with exact and bootstrap inferential summaries and a descriptive Clopper–Pearson bound; (3) concise, artifact-grounded technical clarification of the forbidden-reachability predicate and the validators used; and (4) concrete design lessons and reproducibility guidance to help practitioners and researchers construct follow-up stress tests that actually exercise the repair path.
sections.related_work: Generate–verify–repair and execution-guided repair architectures have improved correctness in code and IaC tasks by using verifier feedback to guide repairs; these systems demonstrate that verifier capability and repair strategy determine realized gains (e.g., TerraFormer and closely related verifier-feedback systems). Survey and NetOps system literature document LLM failure modes—hallucination, overconfidence, domain mismatch—and consistently recommend integrating validators or human oversight. Emulation and testbed work shows execution-based validation is feasible for research-grade evaluation but cautions about external-validity gaps when porting results to production devices or live traffic. Our study addresses a narrower methodological gap: a preregistered paired evaluation with deterministic per-episode validator traces and explicit generation semantics to quantify how experimental-contract choices affect inferential power.
sections.methodology: Preregistered confirmatory design: The preregistration fixed a paired binary design with N = 300 matched intents (150 benign seeds each paired with one programmatic adversarial variant). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Confirmatory test: exact McNemar two-sided test (alpha = 0.05). CIs were prespecified as bootstrap percentile intervals; the final analysis used 10,000 resamples (seed = 1729). Sampling and contamination handling followed preregistered rules (exact duplicates removed; fuzzy duplicates filtered by normalized edit distance threshold). Adapter contract (shared_initial_candidate): to conserve provider usage the run generated a single initial LLM candidate per intent pair and replayed the same candidate to baseline and guarded arms; this yielded model_calls_used = 300 for 300 pairs rather than up to 600 calls for independent-condition generation. Intervention arms: Baseline = shared initial candidate replayed; Guarded = same shared candidate validated by the deterministic validators and allowed up to one repair LLM call if any validator reported forbidden reachability. Validators and forbidden-reachability predicate: two deterministic validators were used—(1) a containerized Batfish-style execution validator that executes/parses configurations in the emulated environment and checks reachability/policy predicates at packet/route semantics level, and (2) a lightweight Python graph-based static reachability analyzer that computes connectivity/policy violations by static graph analysis. The forbidden-reachability predicate is defined operationally as any change that enables previously-blocked flows or otherwise violates the declared access-control reachability constraint for the task; a pair is labeled violating if either validator detects such a predicate (logical OR). Repair policy and determinism: repair was prespecified to allow at most one LLM repair call per pair when triggered; validators and emulator orchestration were implemented deterministically in Docker to ensure replayable per-episode traces.
sections.results: Execution accounting: planned_episode_count = 600 (300 pairs × 2 conditions); completed = 600; failed episodes = 0; model_calls_used = 300 under the shared_initial_candidate contract. Primary confirmatory outcome: baseline_success_count = 300 and guarded_success_count = 300. Paired contingency: n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. McNemar exact two-sided p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the paired risk-difference (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Because no validator ever reported forbidden reachability on the shared initial candidates, the repair path was not invoked in any episode (repair_applied = false for all pairs). The absence of discordant pairs renders the paired McNemar comparison uninformative about repair efficacy: the test requires discordant outcomes to compare conditional probabilities. Descriptive bound: observing 0/300 violations yields a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on an undetected baseline violation rate of approximately 0.00994 (≈0.994%). Validator concordance: the two deterministic validators agreed on all episodes (verifier_disagreement_rate = 0). Representative per-episode traces and aggregated tables (paired contingency and condition summary) are archived in the evidence bundle for auditable verification.
sections.discussion: Statistical interpretation and what the data support: under the exact executed contract (shared_initial_candidate), model (declared: gpt-5-mini), validators, emulator, and adversary generator used here, baseline generation satisfied the forbidden-reachability predicate for every sampled intent; therefore inserting the verifier did not change observed compliance. This empirical fact is robustly supported by the per-episode validator traces and the paired contingency. However, because the repair branch was never exercised, the experiment does not provide evidence that verifier-guided repair can rescue violating initial candidates; the preregistered hypothesis about repair efficacy is untestable in this run. Design lessons (artifact-grounded): (1) Generation semantics matter—shared replay reduces provider cost but also reduces between-arm sampling variability needed to produce discordant violating outputs; to exercise repair efficacy use independent-condition generation (two LLM draws per pair) or increase pair/sample size and repair-call budget. (2) Adversary potency matters—the programmatic adversarial variants used here did not trigger validator-detectable violations; stronger or targeted adversaries are needed to exercise repair paths. (3) Verifier strength and diversity matter—combining multiple, stronger oracles (dynamic execution, route-policy semantics, or production-grade checkers) increases the chance of detecting meaningful violations. (4) Reproducibility is practical—deterministic per-episode traces, provider-call audit, and archived artifacts permit precise accounting and targeted follow-ups. Threats to validity: internal validity is limited by shared_initial_candidate semantics and single-model scope; construct validity depends on whether the forbidden-reachability predicate and the two deterministic validators capture operational security risk; external validity is limited because tasks were synthetic and run in deterministic emulation; conclusion validity is constrained because the observed contingency is degenerate and preregistered power assumptions (nonzero baseline violation rate) are not met.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered, deterministic paired experiment using a shared-initial-candidate contract, two deterministic validators combined by logical OR, and an LLM declared as gpt-5-mini, we observed that both baseline and guarded arms satisfied the forbidden-reachability predicate on all N = 300 matched intents (n11 = 300). The repair path was never invoked; thus the preregistered confirmatory hypothesis that verifier-in-the-loop GVR reduces security-increasing misconfigurations by enabling repair is empirically untestable in this run. The run provides a tight descriptive bound (one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound ≈ 0.00994 on baseline violation rate) and concrete, artifact-grounded design recommendations—use independent-condition generation, stronger adversaries, larger repair budgets, multi-model comparisons, and richer oracles—to construct follow-up experiments that can exercise and evaluate repair efficacy. All core execution and analysis artifacts are archived in the evidence bundle to support reproducibility and targeted stress tests.

limitations: Degenerate confirmatory outcome: zero discordant pairs (n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0) render McNemar inference uninformative about repair efficacy when baseline violation rates are nonzero; the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and targeted detecting a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction.

GVR not exercised: under the chosen task set, emulator, model, and validators the verifier never reported forbidden reachability and consequently the guarded repair step was never invoked; the experiment therefore tests whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant, not whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations.

Generation contract choice: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced one LLM call per pair and reduced model-call overhead but also limited independent draws that could produce discordant errors; alternative contracts (independent-condition generation or expanded repair budgets) would better exercise repair paths.

Adversarial-perturbation detail: the preregistration specified programmatic generation of one adversarial variant per benign seed; per-task generation seeds and intent payloads are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl for reproducibility.

External validity: tasks were synthetically generated and executed in Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation; results do not necessarily generalize to heterogeneous production devices, live traffic conditions, or different operational constraints.
Model and verifier scope: a single model (gpt-5-mini) and two deterministic validators were evaluated; other LLMs, stronger verifiers, or dynamic execution oracles may produce different outcomes.
